item.title: How to Confront the Fear of Being 'That Person'
item.description:
Relationships

How to Confront the Fear of Being 'That Person'

Fitting in isn't belonging. We have to take space to make space for others.

Posted October 31, 2026

Key points
  • The fear of being "that person" can keep us from speaking up about things that matter to us.
  • Fitting in is the demand to minimize our differences, while belonging requires us to share our differences.
  • Conflict avoidance comes at the cost of meaningful recognition and connection.
Source: Illustration by Quiel Ramos

I didn’t want to join the PTA.

My roles as parent, husband, therapist, writer, educator, community helper, and doubles tennis partner already left me no time to pine for more. I didn’t need more meetings or another email thread to colonize my attention. Most of all, I did not want to step out of the comfort of familiar relationships and into potential conflict with people I knew less well.

And yet, I felt I had to. I had concerns about our school community that affected my family and friends deeply, and I wanted to address them.

Like most of my clients and friends, I’m sure you’ve had your own version of this. You identify a concern, consider saying something to the person responsible, rehearse how you might bring it up, and then imagine how it could go wrong.

What if I upset them? What if I’m too much? What if I become… that person?—the nagging, dramatic, irritating person who harshes the group vibe.

So you decide to drop it, play it cool, and say, “Actually, I don’t really care.” Or you speak with an apologetic tone (as if to ask a question, timidly). And as a result, you reject yourself before the other person has the chance to consider your point. Meanwhile, the concern eats away at your insides.

But why do we minimize our needs and desires in the face of others? What are we afraid of?

According to research, people often retreat from conflict out of a fear of losing social inclusion, experiencing rejection, or failing to “fit in” (Brown, 2010).

Fitting In vs. Belonging

Social researcher Brené Brown describes “fitting in” as “assessing a situation and becoming who you need to be to be accepted.” Belonging, on the other hand, “doesn’t require us to change who we are; it requires us to be who we are” (Brown, 2010).

Fitting in demands that we conform to group expectations (e.g., “Gosh, no one argues in this group. Guess I should keep my mouth shut so they don’t think I’m a nag.”). Belonging, in contrast, offers the possibility of finding recognition and connection with the people around us, regardless of our differences. (e.g., “Wow, it’s like that for you? For me it’s more like this.”)

But inviting the possibility of belonging is risky.

Belonging requires us to show up in relationships authentically, even if doing so provokes conflict by default. And when we depend on other people for stability—in a family, group, or community—the stakes of rocking the boat can feel enormous. The fear of losing connection can make retreating in silence seem like the safest option.

article continues after advertisement

But is that always true?

Research on emotional suppression suggests that keeping our feelings hidden doesn’t necessarily improve our relationships. A 2022 study found that expressive suppression was often associated with a weaker relational quality than experienced by those with a more accessible emotional connection (Sasaki, Overall, Chang, & Low, 2022). The study doesn’t suggest that we should be open books, 24/7, but it does show that protecting ourselves and others from our true feelings comes at a great cost to both us and them.

Sometimes “keeping the peace” is simply deferring a necessary conversation that could benefit everyone.

Source: Illustration by Quiel Ramos

Know Your Intention

As both a therapist and a former actor, I think about relationships in terms of scene work: What is my intention? What choices am I making to achieve it? Am I reaching for the person in front of me with an invitation to connect, and to recognize one another—to see and be seen, and to hear and be heard?

Or am I simply protecting myself from rejection and shame—to cover up my fear of “losing” by trying to “win,” to prove that I’m “right” and not “wrong,” or that I’m “good” and not “bad”?

Am I inviting people to see me? Or am I simply trying not to seem like that person?

We can’t control how others receive our invitations, but we can be intentional about how we send those invitations to those around us.

We can identify our context, priorities, and what we want others to understand about us. We can speak from experience, rather than expectations for how all people “should be.” And we can make room for other experiences as well, without hiding, diminishing, or abandoning our own.

This is where the distinction between recognition and agreement (or submission) is essential.

We don’t need our listeners to agree with us to recognize our unique experiences. We don’t need to have the exact same priorities, boundaries, or context to empathize with others and take them seriously.

Research suggests that there are associations between authenticity and positive mental health, and that psychological well-being is primarily connected to our capacity to live in alignment with ourselves (Galinha, Balbino, Devezas, & Trigo, 2023).

article continues after advertisement

We Don’t Have to Choose Between Self Connection and Relational Connection

Of course not every bid for recognition that we make will be fully understood. Some people will feel provoked simply by us showing up as we are. Some people will push back and challenge our voice, and we may need to take a step back, reflect on the dialogue, and decide how to best proceed, perhaps with clearer boundaries and intentions.

But we can begin by recognizing that differences between us are always present, and will always create some degree of conflict each and every time one of us enters a “scene” with another person. Even the people closest to us, whom we love the most, will, in some ways, always be alien to us.

But if we name what those differences are, we create the opportunity for both us and them to show up as fully and freely as possible in one another’s presence.

Speaking up for what we care about may very well rock the boat. And in doing so, we may have to endure periods of being misunderstood, disliked, or being cast as “that person.”

But if we approach each relationship with self-awareness, curiosity, and a deep willingness to see and be seen, to hear and be heard, stepping into potential conflict can become a regular part of creating deeper and more trusting connections with other people.

We don’t do ourselves or anyone else any favors by avoiding being “that person.”

Take Space to Make Space

And just maybe the person we’re afraid of being—the one who speaks up and names concerns at the risk of being disruptive—is exactly the person someone else needs to be invited to speak up themselves.

After my first few days on the PTA, several fellow parents said to me, “Thanks for sharing. I need to practice taking up space like that more often.”

Copyright Mark O'Connell, LCSW-R, MFA

item.title: The Science of Superstition
item.description:
Magical Thinking

The Science of Superstition

Do we steer fate and luck when we are superstitious 迷信?

Posted October 31, 2026

Key points
  • Superstition can be the coalescence of disparate events that happen at the same time.
  • Feeling superstitious may give us a sense of control.
  • That’s why we think ‘oh, bad luck’ when we see a black cat.

My mother was superstitious all her life. We cleaned and dusted the house each Thursday. After that, we could welcome dead ancestors into our home. On Friday afternoons, Mom would place incense sticks in a cup of sand, kneel, and talk to kin who had passed. She would ask them for forgiveness and advice on fixing any wrongness. I surmise that this action made her feel better. She felt comforted, and there is nothing wrong with wanting some comfort.

Superstition and luck go together, though people interpret the two differently. Luck feels more passive, unpredictable, and random, while we have some control over superstition. The superstitious carry a lucky charm to steer fate. We give meaning to disparate events or unrelated coincidences and connect them.

Paul Rozin, a psychology professor at the University of Pennsylvania and former editor of the research journal Appetite, has examined this. He and his colleagues found that people were not amenable to wearing a piece of clothing that had been worn by a murderer, even if it were laundered. The opposite can also be true: When a fan’s item of clothing has been touched and blessed by his favorite celebrity, he would be hard-pressed to launder the item. Rozin found that people are generally superstitious.

Source: AI Assisted

I have my own superstitions 迷信. I wear a headscarf when we visit the graves of our loved ones. In the grand scheme, I don't follow my mother’s rituals and rules, and I shouldn't have to fake my way with a headscarf.

Yet I stand on the soil wearing the scarf anyway. In truth, I feel at ease in this attire at the gravesite. It also reminds me of who I am—in sneakers and a scarf. I am not alone when I use superstitions as a coping strategy.

When situations feel unpredictable or chaotic, superstitious feelings may give us a sense of control. Wearing your lucky socks to a job interview can lower heart rate, tension, stress, and anxiety.

A study in the journal Psychological Science reported that activating superstition, such as signing the cross or throwing salt over the shoulder, can boost confidence and performance. A ritual can be a mental cue that boosts focus, self-efficacy, and self-confidence. Superstitious thinking can also act as a placebo; knocking on wood can improve outlook or performance.

Of course, we cannot go too far. Excessive magical thinking may weaken confidence and agency. Yet many cultures follow rules that are plain wacky; here are some from East Asia:

Don't feed a baby shrimp, mango, or pineapple; he will develop boils

Don’t look at images on the phone; they cause excitement and destabilize energy

Close the bathroom door; evil spirits are in the toilet

Fold clothes, don't hang them; a ghost can put on the clothes

Don't sleep with a mirror near the bed; it decreases yang energy

article continues after advertisement

And if you are pregnant:

Don't hammer nails in the wall; it causes fetal malformation

Don't sew on the bed—needle, scissors give the baby cleft palate

Don't dig in the garden; it causes mental disturbance for the baby

Don't raise your hand above your head; it's bad energy for the fetus

Avoid dark foods——the baby will develop dark skin from chocolate, cola, coffee, or others

item.title: Takeaways From 'The New Stanford Prison Experiment'
item.description:
Leadership

Takeaways From 'The New Stanford Prison Experiment'

Netflix's new reality series is fraught with problems and compelling to watch.

Posted October 31, 2026

Key points
  • A recent Netflix series presents a simulation of the Stanford Prison Experiment (SPE).
  • There are some similarities between the new Netflix reality show and the original SPE.
  • The reality show explores how identity intersects with power, leadership, and perceptions of authority.
  • Contestants' awareness of being on TV complicates authenticity and ethical validity.

This is Part 2 of a two-part series. Read Part 1 here.

While I attempted to approach "The New Stanford Prison Experiment," a newly released Netflix reality television series, with an open mind, I couldn’t help but identify from the start significant distinctions between the study originally conducted by Philip Zimbardo and his graduate students in 1971 and the conditions the architects of this reimagining put in place.

As I reflected on in Part 1 of this series, this show in no way meets the scientific criteria for sanctioned research. The fact of its being produced and recorded for television—and presumably, for entertainment purposes—introduces the fraught variable of how individuals recruited will react knowing it will be viewed by the larger public, in addition to the obvious lack of any IRB approval regarding the ethics of this simulation.

While Zimbardo screened prospective volunteers for his study in an effort to ensure they could handle the potentially stressful 14-day interval of the simulation, it remains unclear how individuals were recruited for this show, and dubious that random assignment was used to decide who would play the role of guards versus prisoners. In fact, at least two of the “inmates” on this show share in their self-narrations having had brushes with the law, with at least one reporting having been incarcerated. This individual clearly shows signs of being retraumatized by the conditions of the simulated prison in Episode 1, which is actually filmed in a real prison.

One of the dimensions of this reality show that distinguishes watching it from the experience of being exposed to the original footage of the actual study is that the Netflix contestants are housed in an actual correctional facility rather than in the makeshift prison of the 1971 study. Imagination is not required for individuals on this show to feel as if they are incarcerated, because they are in fact in an actual prison, even if they have been separated from other inmates, correctional officers, and staff.

So, while all the participants are aware they consented to participate in this reality show—curiously, many contestants repeatedly refer to their taking part in this “experiment,” despite it not reflecting sanctioned research—it is not only the roles they have been assigned that create the conditions of being incarcerated but also the literal environment they have been placed in. The uniforms the guards and prisoners are clothed in serve as additional social cues reminding them of their respective positions—similar to the way Zimbardo leveraged such costumes to trigger authenticity in the experience for each participant. It is clear in watching this production that the budget was greater than what Zimbardo had at his disposal, and that such resources were allocated to create authenticity for the contestants so that the simulation felt like actual incarceration.

Perhaps the most engaging element of this reality show is that the contestants reflect a more diverse group of people than the original sample, offering a dimension not present in Zimbardo’s study. Zimbardo’s sample consisted exclusively of traditionally aged white male college students, while the individuals recruited for this show reflect diversity in race and age, and include three women. All three women—two of color—are assigned the role of correctional officers, presumably for the logistical complexity of housing one or more women in a pod of 20-plus males.

article continues after advertisement

The inclusion of women and Black males offers a further layer of complexity regarding how identity intersects with power and perceptions of authority and leadership. In fact, the female guards explicitly reflect on their gender when they self-narrate how they are navigating their roles over the course of the experience. While the male guards generally approach leadership with a sense of entitlement, the female guards are sensitive to having to “earn” legitimacy in their positions, perhaps best exemplified by a scene shown more than once from an early episode when one of the male guards repeatedly speaks over a female one who is attempting to relay information to the larger group of guards by reading a missive left for the group.

Another element less salient in Zimbardo’s study is the openness with which contestants in this simulation—both assigned inmates and guards—reflect on leadership and how it develops. In fact, over the course of this simulation, abuse of power is a far less salient feature of the group dynamics that develop than which members are perceived as effective versus ineffective leaders. Both explicit and implicit norms develop regarding hierarchies within both groups, as engaging intragroup and intergroup dynamics emerge.

Lastly, this reality show specifically breaks up the experience of the contestants into four phases, diverging significantly from the original study design. The four phases are referred to as: transformation, hierarchy, role-reversal, and self-governance. Each phase reflects an escalation of uncertainty in conditions imposed on the contestants, becoming more outrageous with each new iteration they are exposed to. Notably, each phase is further marked by at least one contestant opting out of continuing the simulation by evoking “pineapple,” the safe word all participants have been told will enable them to be extracted from the prison if or when they feel uncomfortable or unsafe prior to the 14-day mark.

“Transformation” reflects the first stage of the simulation, when contestants learn what role they have been assigned and start to transition into their respective roles as prisoner or guard within the facility. This interval of the simulation is perhaps most true to the original study. From there, the show diverges; even the pretense of scientific replication has been discarded, and contestants are exposed to ever more extreme conditions. In the “hierarchy” phase, both guards and inmates are placed in positions where individuals from their ranks are explicitly placed in leadership positions. This phase demonstrates noteworthy friction that develops between the guards, as each shift has to select a specific leader within their subgroup, and then announce their decision to the pod of inmates. The last two phases become more extreme in what contestants are exposed to, starkly reminding both viewers and participants that this very clearly is a reality production and not a scientific experiment.

article continues after advertisement

While there is much to reflect on regarding this series, the extent to which this Netflix show repositions the Stanford Prison Experiment or offers any new insights in this regard is questionable. In fact, I would argue the release of this show perhaps best exemplifies the enduring interest of the original study, as the question of whether or not and how power corrupts individuals when operating as part of a larger collective is just as resonant today as it was in Zimbardo’s day. An additional question to consider, especially in light of this particular reimagining, is whether or how entertainment corrupts—is it possible to produce authentic reactions in individuals experiencing a simulation when they know they are being recorded for a television series?

Alas, readers interested in the answer to this question will have to watch the show and decide for themselves.

Copyright 2026 Azadeh Aalai

item.title: What Is 'Black Cat' Energy in Dating?
item.description:
Mating

What Is 'Black Cat' Energy in Dating?

A somewhat aloof love interest can be a turnoff, a challenge, or true catnip.

Posted October 31, 2026

Key points
  • "Black cat" energy is when someone manifests the classic stereotypical persona of a black cat.
  • This persona may be calm, reserved, independent, and even aloof, prone to setting clear boundaries.
  • It can take a lot to win a black cat's trust. But once that happens, the black cat can be very loyal.
  • Black cat behaviors can be quite attractive but can also be turnoffs, especially when taken to extremes.
When someone has "black cat" energy, that person embodies the classic stereotypical persona of the black cat.
Source: Maycon Alves/Pexels

Say you are on a first date and the person seems rather reserved and not super enthusiastic about you. Don't let it spook you prematurely. Because rather than a cat-astrophic situation, it could actually be a cat situation—as in someone with "black cat" energy.

What Is a 'Black Cat' Girlfriend or Boyfriend

You may have seen references to "black cat girlfriends" or "black cat boyfriends" on social media and other parts of the internet. These probably aren't referring to real black cats—unless some calico somewhere has somehow been posting like crazy. No, these terms describe human significant others who have "black cat" energy—meaning they embody the classic stereotypical personas of black cats.

What Is 'Black Cat' Energy?

So what exactly is the classic persona of a black cat? Well, it's a calm, reserved, and potentially introverted persona. Many black cats are known, too, for acting quite independent and self-assured—seemingly not needing validation from others. All of this can make them appear rather aloof.

The stereotype also has black cats establishing and maintaining fairly clear boundaries until you prove yourself worthy. It's about their tending to be very selective about whom they offer their time, effort, and affection to and to not open up until you've earned their trust. However, the stereotype is that once you've earned that trust, black cats can be very loyal.

Oh, and if you want a black cat to chase after you or in some way suck up to you, this classic persona says fuggedaboudit—that a black cat can't be bothered to do any of that. That may be leaving you either a bit confused or convinced that the black cat has no romantic interest in you. Meanwhile, the black cat may be thinking, "Well, I am continuing to communicate with you and showed up so far. Isn't that enough to show some interest?"

The Advantages of Having Black Cat Dating Energy

All of this can make someone with such stereotypical black cat energy quite attractive. After all, you know how many people like a mystery and a challenge. Those who have such black cat energy also may be less likely to lose themselves in a relationship. They'll continue to maintain their hobbies, friends, and other interests. That can leave them more grounded and even-keeled with a better sense of self—more things that can be attractive.

article continues after advertisement

Since those with such black cat energy are much more selective in whom they get close to, once you've formed a solid bond with them, it can be all the more solid. What you see is what you get as well. They may not be as likely to tell you something to simply make you feel good.

The Disadvantages of Having Black Cat Dating Energy

Everything is not purr-fect with such black cats, though, especially if they take their black cat behaviors to the extreme. Their hard-to-get-to-know personas can leave many people not bothering to get to know them. Black cat energy can come across as being too cold and distant. Others may desire more emotional feedback and assurance. As a result, the only people pursuing a black cat might be those simply wanting a challenge.

As well, there can be fine lines between appearing reserved, being aloof, and seeming downright arrogant. The black cat energy can end up rubbing people the wrong way. It might elicit some "Oh, so you think you are better than me" responses.

Additionally, being too black catty, so to speak, can inhibit the development of deep relationships. Others may not be willing to wait so long and work so hard to earn someone's acceptance. Black cats may find that no one can pass their very high standards.

What to Do If You Are the Black Cat

If you are a so-called black cat, it makes sense to embrace, further enhance, and even celebrate your many aforementioned strengths. Don't settle for less than you deserve. Dating is about finding the right mutual fit, and there are people out there who appreciate what you have to offer.

At the same time, beware of having too much of a black "cattitude." Realize that no relationship should be about one person proving themselves to the other. It's better to meet each other somewhere in the middle and compromise. And don't wait too long to let someone into your circle of trust.

Consider offering more positive feedback, as well. Show that you appreciate others' efforts. A little encouragement can go a long way.

article continues after advertisement

What to Do With a Black Cat

And what should you do if the other person is the black cat? Well, first, it helps to recognize their black cattiness and realize that they fall into another cat-tegory. The normal rules may not apply here.

Remind yourself that actions speak louder than words. Don't expect the same reassurances that others may give. If black cats keep showing up for dates when you ask them and respond to your messages, such actions may be enough to demonstrate their continued interest. You may have to do a little more than you are accustomed to doing to nudge things along.

And trying to control or micromanage a black cat can be one of the worst things that you can do. When you give them the requisite freedom and respect, they could respond with some more playful licks—figuratively speaking, of course.

Finally, keep the lines of communication open. Don't be afraid to tell the black cat how all that black cat energy makes you feel—both good and bad. Such authenticity and earnestness can help win the black cat over and cat-apault your connection to another level.

item.title: Empathy, and Why Reading a Novel Can Make Us Cry
item.description:
Empathy

Empathy, and Why Reading a Novel Can Make Us Cry

'Sorrow and Bliss' by Meg Mason engages the reader in others' emotional lives.

Posted October 31, 2026

Key points
  • Experiencing empathy is one of the best reasons for reading a novel.
  • The brain's empathy systems are a part of the concept of "theory of mind."
  • Mind reading is another way of thinking about theory of mind.

Well, I have already broken my promise to post my second blog post a few days after my introductory post, and after that, once a month. Let’s see if I can at least stick, sort of, to the once-a-month plan.

Source: Jenni Ogden

Right next to me now is the print copy of Meg Mason’s stunning second novel, Sorrow and Bliss, first published in Australia in 2020, which was shortlisted for the Women’s Prize for Fiction in 2022 and won other big awards. The image on the cover is lovely, but the real thing is tactile: a perfect cover, still with a new-book perfume years after I purchased it. I am a reader who does not turn down page corners or leave my precious books in the sun—except for the four minutes I took to take this photo of the book lying in our garden! On the title page, Meg has signed my copy; I purchased it after her session at the Auckland Writers Festival in 2024; I have shelves of books, some signed, some not, purchased at that same incredible festival. Sorrow and Bliss rightly became a major bestseller (as I think her latest novel, Sophie, Standing There (published in August this year), also will. (Meg grew up in New Zealand and has lived in Australia since a teenager. But she identifies first as a Kiwi (just saying…).

Goodreads describes Sorrow and Bliss thus: This novel is about a 40-year-old woman called Martha. She knows there is something wrong with her but she doesn't know what it is. Her husband Patrick thinks she is fine. He says everyone has something, the thing is just to keep going.

Martha told Patrick before they got married that she didn't want to have children. He said he didn't mind either way because he has loved her since he was fourteen and making her happy is all that matters, although he does not seem able to do it.

By the time Martha finds out what is wrong, it doesn't really matter anymore. It is too late to get the only thing she has ever wanted. Or maybe it will turn out that you can stop loving someone and start again from nothing—if you can find something else to want.

There were many reasons why I loved this novel, most psychological, but I think empathy is the emotion that is overarching and, from a psychologist’s point of view, could provide a reason for why we read novels. It is a wonderful writer who can write words and sentences and stories that are so vivid we can imagine and feel every part of those emotions that the characters are feeling.

article continues after advertisement

Our brains are wired to respond to other people’s emotions almost as if we are experiencing them ourselves; for example, studies have shown that when we observe someone else doing something or showing an emotion that engages us, the same neurons fire in our brains as would fire if we were feeling a similar emotion. These have been called mirror neurons. In fact, many systems in our brains are connected with empathy, which in turn is part of the concept called theory of mind; the cognitive capacity that humans have that allows them to attribute mental states, including thoughts and feelings, to oneself as well as to others (mind reading!) [see my past post on this]. Meg Mason’s novel effortlessly invites us in and permits us to read the mind of Martha. Writers call this writerly skill "showing, not telling."

Razor-sharp, laugh-aloud funny, and shatteringly sad, Martha’s story will not let you go. At 40, her life has split asunder, her marriage unable to survive the weight of her lifelong mental illness that no doctors or medications have been able to diagnose or fix. Just keeping going isn’t working for her or her husband.

As a reader and certainly as a psychologist, it is almost impossible not to try and guess what the mental illness is that Martha has struggled with for most of her life. But it remained unnamed. Finally, on page 233, Martha's new psychiatrist names it, but all the reader sees on the page is a dash. From then on, as Martha tries to talk about this diagnosis she finally has with her husband and family, every time the "disorder" is mentioned, all we get is that dash. What an incredible way to highlight the downsides of "labelling," especially when a label stamps a person with a condition or a characteristic that forces them into being someone they are not, because nobody is a single thing. So Martha’s life cannot be pinned to whatever our idea might be of whatever disorder we think she might have, and instead we are encouraged to see the ripple effects of her chronic struggle that tests the love she feels for her family and they for her and even pushes her to sabotage her own relationships even when she is deeply loved.

Novels these days are sometimes accompanied by "red flag" warnings signaling that the content may be triggering for some readers. My "red flag" for this book would be to ensure you have a box of tissues close by. But you will be giggling as well. What more can we ask of a good read?

Previous blog posts inspired by writers I heard at the Auckland Writers Festival include:

  1. The Sebastian Barry moment.
  2. The Lloyd Geering talk when he was 99; he is now 108 and still writing and speaking. (Another of my beliefs: Writing and reading are good for the brain and help us live long and healthy lives!)

Happy reading, and catch you in a month (or thereabouts)!

item.title: Gay Men: Are We Living a Good Life or Is Something Missing?
item.description:
Singlehood

Gay Men: Are We Living a Good Life or Is Something Missing?

Personal Perspective: Heteronormativity affects how we measure our lives.

Posted October 31, 2026

Key points
  • Heteronormativity connects to broader social hierarchies of worth that value some ways of living over others.
  • People can reinforce heteronormative expectations without consciously holding homophobic beliefs.
  • We all internalize familial and cultural expectations, and examining them requires conscious effort.
Source: Nate Bash / Unsplash

I recently flew home for my aunt's surprise 70th birthday party. It was a beautiful celebration, full of family, laughter, and lots of good food and catching up.

I love my family, and I know they love me.

Still, whenever I visit home, I’m often asked whether I’m dating, and if not, why not. I regularly hear talk of who bought a new home or recently got married.

Meanwhile, I’ve had a pretty full year. Last October, I got licensed as a therapist, and that same month, I received a publishing contract for my second book. I’ve also been spending time exploring the possibility of living in Mexico City, nurturing a strong spiritual life, and focusing on my health.

Writing my second book has been a passion project of mine. I was recently telling a friend that so much of writing isn’t even writing. The stories and experiences a person is writing about have to be lived first. A book is an extension of the writer’s life, and mine reflects my life and the passion I feel about my work.

I've also been single for a long time, and I used to believe something was wrong with me for not being in a relationship. I’ve even explored my propensity for being single in therapy. I've turned over a lot of rocks, and what I’ve discovered is that I'm happily single.

Many gay men leave their hometowns to find community in larger cities, where there's greater access to other gay people and more affirming environments. It's part of what brought me to Los Angeles.

While I was home, I kept wondering why so few people asked me about my book, my work, what it’s been like starting a private practice, my spiritual interests, or my love of traveling and my dream of living in Mexico City. What’s more, when I did try to talk about these things, it seemed as though there wasn’t as much interest as there was in kids, weddings, and new houses. What I’ve been reflecting on since is how heteronormativity can influence the questions even the most loving people think to ask.

By the time I left, I found myself wondering if something was wrong with my life. I'm not married, I don't have children, and I live alone. Yet when I'm in Los Angeles, I don't feel lonely or that anything is missing.

When I got back to LA, I told a friend about the trip and admitted how much the experience had made me question my life. Was I the lonely single gay man living in a big city without a family? As we talked, he told me he’s felt similarly whenever he’s visited family back home. I hear the same thing from many of the gay men I work with in my practice.

article continues after advertisement

What I realized is that I chose not to have children, and I’m choosing to be single. I’ve also never had a desire to own a home. None of these things mean my life is lacking. What I had been feeling was the weight of heteronormativity’s unconscious demands, projections, and expectations.

What Is Heteronormativity?

Heteronormativity, the assumption that heterosexuality and heterosexual relationships are the norm, is a lens through which many people perceive what a person's life is supposed to look like, including whether they are married, have children, or own a home.

Heteronormativity is connected to broader social hierarchies of worth, in which society assigns greater value to certain ways of living than others. These assumptions can operate even when someone doesn't consciously hold homophobic beliefs.

It reminds me of an episode of Sex and the City called “A Woman’s Right to Shoes.” At a baby shower, Carrie takes off her shoes at her friend’s request, only to discover that they’ve been stolen. When her friend refuses to replace them, Carrie points out how much money she has spent celebrating her friends’ weddings, anniversaries, and children. She eventually registers for gifts to celebrate her “marriage to herself” and asks her friend for the shoes.

The episode raises an interesting question about whose life choices we celebrate and whose we question. Why are marriage and children milestones that deserve gifts and celebration, while a single person’s choices and interests can be treated as less worthy of the same recognition?

Heteronormativity informs how we think, and how we think informs our beliefs. Our beliefs, in turn, inform the questions we ask and how curious we are about another person's life. The more our thinking is filtered through heteronormativity, the more likely we are to misunderstand someone else's life. Depending on what we believe is normal, we can unconsciously project our opinions and judgments onto others.

Most of my family is straight, and while their questions come from love, they also reflect heteronormativity, which can limit what they’re able to see beyond their own experiences.

Across generations, gay and straight people have been taught that a successful life means getting married, having children, and buying a home. Surrounded by these societal expectations, it can be easy for many gay men to feel as if we're falling short, not measuring up, or that our lives are missing something essential.

When we absorb other people's projections without recognizing them, we can measure our lives against heteronormative ideals that don’t align with our personal values, desires, or interests.

The next time you find yourself wondering whether something is missing from your life, I’d invite you to consider what you want for your life—not what you think you should want.

For those who love the gay men in their lives, I invite you to get curious about the fullness of our lives, including our work, our passions, our friendships, and anything else that makes us come alive. You may discover that the life you were worried about is fuller than you imagined.
